article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Balanced hybrid
Genetics: Equatorial Sativa × Middle Eastern Indica
Breeder: Joint Doctor / High-Bred Seeds
THC Content: 18-20%
CBD Content: Not officially specified
Terpene Profile: myrcene , caryophyllene , limonene
Primary Flavors: Sweet musk, earth, hash, pine, herbs
Flowering Time (Indoor): 60–65 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Mid-October
Indoor Yield: 400–500 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Moderate
Grow Difficulty: Easy

Dreadlock earned its name in the garden rather than through creative marketing. Its unusually large central flowers develop into thick, irregular formations that resemble tightly packed locks, giving the cultivar a recognizable appearance long before modern cannabis breeding became filled with elaborate strain names. Created by the Joint Doctor, the Canadian breeder best known for his later work with autoflowering genetics, Dreadlock is an older photoperiod hybrid made from an equatorial sativa female and a Middle Eastern indica male.

The pairing creates an almost perfect balance between two very different cannabis traditions: tropical-style cerebral energy on one side and heavier, resinous indica structure on the other. Period cultivation information describes a hardy plant that resists mold and pests, requires relatively little fertilizer, and can produce approximately 400–500 grams per square meter indoors. The finished weed is equally distinctive, combining sweet musk and hash-like earthiness with an effect that begins slowly before developing into an energetic, social, almost psychedelic high.
Genetics and Lineage

The original breeder-era pedigree identifies Dreadlock as an equatorial sativa female crossed with a Middle Eastern indica male. The source material does not assign familiar commercial strain names to either parent, which makes the geographic description the most accurate way to document the lineage. Period genetic records independently preserve the same formula and identify the breeder as Joint Doctor’s High-Bred Seeds. Claims assigning modern named parents to Dreadlock therefore should be treated cautiously unless they can be traced to an authenticated breeding record.

Those two parental directions explain the unusually balanced character of the plant. Equatorial cannabis populations generally contribute greater cerebral activity, longer branching tendencies, and an energetic mental effect, while traditional Middle Eastern genetics are associated with denser flowers, resin production, shorter maturation, and stronger physical relaxation. Dreadlock manages to express both without behaving like an extreme example of either category. The original specification calls it a 50/50 indica-sativa hybrid and documents two main phenotypes: one forms somewhat fluffier flowers with numerous smaller bud sites, while the other branches less and creates denser colas. Both share the giant central flower structure responsible for the strain’s name.

The cultivar is also an interesting part of Joint Doctor’s history because it predates the autoflowering work for which the breeder later became internationally famous. Joint Doctor subsequently became closely associated with Lowryder and the development of compact, fast-cycle cannabis, but interviews show that his breeding interests had always included unusual plant characteristics and geographically diverse genetics. Dreadlock reflects that earlier experimental approach in a conventional photoperiod plant.
Effects and Experience

Patience matters when judging the Dreadlock high. The original description specifically calls it a creeper, meaning the first several minutes may not reveal its eventual strength. Mental energy builds gradually during roughly the first half hour, moving from a mild change in perception toward a noticeably more stimulating state. At its peak, breeder-era descriptions characterize the experience as energetic, social, psychedelic, and slightly speedy. Conversation can become unusually entertaining, ordinary observations seem more interesting, and laughter tends to come easily.

That cerebral activity does not completely eliminate the indica side. A calmer physical foundation sits underneath the brighter head effects, preventing moderate amounts from feeling entirely frantic. This makes Dreadlock an unusual social cultivar: mentally animated but physically comfortable. Music, informal gatherings, outdoor recreation, gaming, films, or creative activities fit the experience better than situations requiring perfectly organized thinking. The strain earned a reputation for “giggle stick” qualities because its combination of stimulation and relaxation can encourage prolonged conversation and laughter.

Higher doses make the psychedelic and distracting side more pronounced. Time perception may become less dependable and thoughts can wander substantially, making driving or precision work inappropriate. Since the original breeder specification did not publish a standardized THC percentage, consumers should rely on testing of the actual flower rather than assuming every preserved Dreadlock plant has the same potency.
Medical Benefits

Dreadlock may appeal to medical cannabis consumers who prefer mentally uplifting weed over strongly sedating evening cultivars. The gradual increase in energy and sociability can make this type of marijuana attractive during periods of temporary low mood, stress, or reduced motivation. At the same time, the Middle Eastern indica influence contributes enough physical ease that the experience is not purely stimulating. Some consumers may also notice increased appetite as the high develops.

Its unusually social character may be appealing to people who find certain heavy cannabis varieties isolating or mentally dulling. Nevertheless, stimulating THC-rich cannabis can have the opposite effect in sensitive individuals, potentially increasing anxiety, rapid heartbeat, restlessness, or mental distraction. Dose is therefore especially important with a cultivar whose effects continue becoming stronger well after the first inhalation.

Dreadlock itself has not been evaluated in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for depression, anxiety, chronic pain, appetite disorders, or another medical condition. Medical users should consider laboratory testing of the specific product and appropriate healthcare advice rather than treating historical strain effects as established medical outcomes.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Sweet musk defines the classic Dreadlock fragrance. Period breeder information describes the cultivar as sweet and mildly musky, while its heavy resin and Middle Eastern influence introduce additional earth, herbs, hash, and dry spice. Rather than smelling like modern fruit candy, the sweetness is warmer and more organic, sitting against unmistakably traditional marijuana aromas.

Grinding the sticky flower releases a stronger resinous character. Pine, earth, dried herbs, and a hash-like musk can become more apparent, while some examples develop a slightly sharper or fuel-like edge. The inhale tends to begin smoother and sweeter before moving toward earth and resin on the finish. This makes Dreadlock a particularly appropriate cultivar for consumers who prefer traditional cannabis flavor over cream, pastry, or candy-dominant profiles.

No standardized terpene analysis was included with the original seed line. Myrcene would be consistent with musky earth, pinene with the fresher evergreen side, caryophyllene with spice, and limonene or terpinolene could contribute brighter elements found in more sativa-oriented phenotypes. These remain aromatic associations rather than a universal laboratory formula.
Growing Information

Dreadlock was specifically recommended for newer cultivators because it combines vigor with relatively simple nutritional requirements. The breeder noted that heavy feeding is unnecessary for the plant to produce substantial flowers, while natural resistance to mold and pests provides additional tolerance for imperfect environments. Organic soil was Joint Doctor’s preferred method, although hydroponic cultivation was also reported to work well.

Its structure allows several different indoor strategies. Each plant tends to develop a large central cola, making Sea of Green practical, but the breeder considered Screen of Green especially effective. Allowing roughly one square foot per plant improves production, with historical indoor figures reaching approximately 400–500 g/m². Dreadlock also roots rapidly from cuttings and quickly develops bushy foliage, making healthy females particularly useful as mother plants for growers maintaining clones.

Flowering requires approximately 60–65 days. Cutting early is one of the easiest ways to lose quality because the breeder specifically noted that buds gain considerable weight and potency during their final weeks. A full nine weeks is therefore preferable when plant maturity supports it. Mature fan leaves naturally yellow and drop away, reducing the amount of foliage that must be removed during harvest. Another unusual visual trait is the presence of small horn-shaped leaflets near the bases of the cultivar’s dark, nine-pronged fan leaves.

Outdoor maturity occurs around mid-October at approximately 46° north latitude according to the original specification. Mold resistance is helpful as autumn weather becomes damp, though dense flowers still benefit from good airflow and regular inspection. No trustworthy original outdoor yield figure survives, so claims assigning a specific number of ounces or grams to every plant should be treated as modern estimates rather than breeder specifications.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Dreadlock?

Dreadlock was created from an equatorial sativa female and a Middle Eastern indica male. The original breeder-era description classifies the finished cultivar as an even 50% sativa and 50% indica hybrid.
Who bred the Dreadlock strain?
Dreadlock was produced by the Joint Doctor under Joint Doctor’s High-Bred Seeds. The breeder later became internationally famous for Lowryder and early commercial autoflowering cannabis genetics.
Why is it called Dreadlock?

The name comes from the plant’s unusual flower structure. Both documented phenotypes tend to produce an exceptionally large central cola with dense, irregular bud formations that resemble a large dreadlock.
How long does Dreadlock take to flower?
Indoor flowering lasts approximately 60–65 days. The breeder recommended allowing a complete nine-week cycle because the flowers gain significant weight and potency during the final portion of bloom.
Is Dreadlock easy to grow?

Yes. The original breeder description specifically recommends it for beginning growers. Dreadlock requires relatively modest fertilizer levels, shows good resistance to molds and pests, clones easily, and performs in both organic soil and hydroponic systems.
Final Thoughts on Dreadlock

Dreadlock is an excellent example of a strain whose personality comes directly from its breeding rather than from a fashionable name. Equatorial sativa genetics supply the increasingly energetic, cerebral, and social high, while the Middle Eastern indica parent contributes resin, flower density, resilience, and physical calm. The combination produces weed that can feel relaxed at first before gradually developing into a much brighter and almost psychedelic experience.

Growers gain equally practical traits. Dreadlock flowers in roughly nine weeks, can produce around 400–500 g/m² indoors, tolerates relatively light feeding, resists common garden problems, roots quickly from clones, and works particularly well with Screen of Green cultivation. Its large central colas and unusual fan-leaf details give the plant a recognizable physical identity in addition to its effects.

Although Joint Doctor later became far better known for revolutionary autoflowering genetics, Dreadlock demonstrates that his earlier photoperiod work deserves attention of its own. Sweet musk, hashy earth, sticky flowers, creeping cerebral energy, and straightforward cultivation give this balanced Canadian hybrid a character that remains distinct from both modern high-THC dessert marijuana strains and the autoflowering cultivars that ultimately made its breeder famous.
